/how-i-build::have you ever broken one o.text: These six principles came out of decisions I had to make on real flows, most of them on the AI Service Booking Agent, so they're arguable rather than dogma — but they haven't been ones I've broken in the work described here. /how-i-build::where did these come from.text: These six principles came out of real decisions I had to make on actual builds — most of them while building the AI Service Booking Agent. Each one was forced by a concrete choice on a real flow, not written up in the abstract, and each is arguable — I'm happy to argue any of them.

/how-i-build::which is most contentious.text: Of the six, "pick a metric that can prove you wrong" is the one I'd call most contentious — it directly attacks vendor-published IVR abandonment benchmarks as marketing figures with no traceable primary source, and insists you measure your own call log instead. That's a stance against an industry's standard reference points, not just a build preference.

/work/airtel::what does the validation l.text: The validation layer runs before an order can move forward in Siebel's real-time discount integration, catching bad discount data at order capture. Without it, an order carrying bad discount data wouldn't fail loudly — it would fail downstream in fulfilment and billing, after the customer had already been told yes.

/work/airtel::what drove the 17%.text: The entries attribute the 17% client revenue uplift to the Airtel engagement as a whole rather than breaking out a single cause — that work included the real-time discount integration on order capture, the validation layer keeping bad orders out of billing, 20+ change requests, 10+ workflow automations, and 8+ Open UI customisations. I don't have a further breakdown of which piece drove the number specifically.

/work/airtel::what else shipped there.text: Alongside the real-time discount integration and its validation layer, I delivered 20+ change requests across applets, views and business components, built 10+ workflows automating customer onboarding and request handling, and did 8+ Open UI customisations using PR/PM and JavaScript. That work contributed to a 17% client revenue uplift, ~15% page load improvement, and 60+ defects resolved at >95% SLA adherence.

/work/booking-agent::how is this differe.text: An IVR can't handle "Thursday if you've got something" — it needs rigid menu options. My booking agent uses a deterministic state machine in code for the actual logic, with the LLM confined to one narrow job: turning a spoken sentence into a small JSON object, so it can understand natural, flexible speech without the model ever driving the flow or seeing customer data. It also treats barge-in and sub-second first audio as requirements from the start, which is what makes it feel like a conversation rather than a phone tree.

/work/booking-agent::when will it be don.text: The booking agent's backend, schema, and capacity model are already built and verified — the business-rules layer is in progress. I haven't given a completion date on this site; if you need a firm timeline, email me at shashankjindal1306@gmail.com.

/work/booking-agent::why shouldn't the m.text: Because business rules that live in a prompt are business rules you can't test. In the booking agent, a deterministic state machine in code decides what happens next; the LLM's only job is turning a spoken sentence into a small JSON object, never deciding logic, seeing customer data, or writing prose. That constraint is also what makes an on-premise deployment possible, which is often the reason an enterprise buyer says yes.

/work/dhobi-dash::how did you find the f.text: A shop owner two streets away handed me six paper registers and asked me to find an order from the previous month — that's what showed me how these businesses actually run. I built the product around that constraint and sold it to him the same week I finished it. Six more shops followed within three months, and all seven are still active on monthly retainers.

/work/dhobi-dash::what keeps the data cl.text: In Dhobi Dash, the business rules are enforced rather than advised: an order can't be marked delivered while a balance is outstanding, delivered orders become read-only once completed, a payment can't exceed what's pending, and a duplicate phone number is rejected on entry. Those constraints are what keep seven shops' data from getting corrupted during a morning rush.

/work/dhobi-dash::why an ai builder.text: For Dhobi Dash, the risk was never the code — it was whether a shop owner would actually change how he works. So I put my time into discovery and the spec, and used an AI builder to get from spec to a working product in a week, which let me sell it to the owner with six paper registers that same week.

/work/hero::what did that trade off.text: Moving Hero's lead ingestion off the business layer and onto the extension schema meant giving up the validation and event logic that layer would normally apply. That trade-off is deliberate: it's correct at 100,000 records a day, but wrong at low volume, so validation has to happen before the data ever arrives rather than being caught in transit.

/work/hero::what was the outcome.text: On the Hero lead-migration work, the outcome has been zero reported issues since it went to production. It also collapsed roughly ten thousand daily EAI invocations into a single nightly job moving around 100,000 lead records.

/work/hero::why bypass the business laye.text: Because at 100,000 lead records a day, routing through Siebel's business layer via EAI meant roughly ten thousand separate runs to move one day's data — slow, fragile, and competing with everything else on the instance. Writing directly to the SIEBELEXT extension schema and moving it in a single nightly job at 22:00 collapsed that to one run. The trade-off is real: you give up the validation and event logic the business layer would have applied, so validation has to happen upstream before the data arrives. That's correct at this volume and wrong at low volume — it's a deliberate, scale-specific call, not a general pattern.

The same pattern applies to other document sets: policies, manuals, or records, wired with access controls appropriate to who should see them. If you want to talk through whether it fits your specific documents, email me at shashankjindal1306@gmail.com.

/work/hr-policy-assistant::how does it s.text: The HR Policy Assistant answers only by retrieving from the company's actual policy documents and citing which document each answer came from, so the reader can verify it. If a question isn't covered by that corpus, it declines to answer rather than guessing — that refusal behavior was designed in from the start, not bolted on afterward.

/work/hr-policy-assistant::what happens.text: When a question isn't covered by the HR policy documents, the assistant declines and says nothing further — it doesn't guess or invent an answer. That refusal behavior was designed in from the start, not bolted on after the fact; the interesting part of a grounded system is what it refuses, not just what it answers.

/work/tdd-generator::how does the output.text: The TDD Generator is schema-driven — it takes a CR ID, description, and object list and maps them into a fixed structure, so the output format is the same every time regardless of who's running it. That's what makes it consistent across people and ready for downstream automation, rather than producing a wall of free-form prose.

/work/tdd-generator::is it live.text: Yes — the Siebel TDD Generator is live at tdd-generator.fly.dev. It does what it's built to do; I haven't claimed any usage or adoption numbers for it.

/work/tdd-generator::what problem does i.text: The Siebel TDD Generator solves the problem of Technical Design Documents costing hours of repetitive formatting per change request — the actual thinking takes twenty minutes, but writing it up takes an afternoon. It takes a CR ID, a description and a free-text object list, and generates a structured, schema-driven TDD in seconds, so the output is consistent and ready for downstream automation instead of a wall of prose.

/work/voltas::what does the monitoring c.text: The Voltas monitoring tool (voltasmon) gives a single view across eight component groups: application interface tier, app servers, cluster and nodes, gateway server, Siebel servers, database, OBIEE, and miscellaneous services. Per node it reports CPU, memory and disk, component status, JVM heap, and inbound SOAP and REST call counts shown as successful against total, plus environment switching, per-node refresh timestamps, and an admin config surface. It's an internal tool with no public link.
